title: Theism
wiki_lead:
Theism is belief in God or gods. In a narrow sense, it refers to belief in a single creator deity who is all-powerful, all-knowing, and all-benevolent. A god is a powerful being, often understood as a conscious and immortal person, but the exact characterization and divine attributes vary by tradition. Theism contrasts with nontheism and atheism, which involve the absence or rejection of belief in gods, and with agnosticism, which holds that the existence of gods is unknown or unknowable.
Types of theism can be distinguished by the number of gods they affirm: monotheism accepts only one god, whereas polytheism believes in several gods. Another classification focuses on the relation between the divine and the world. Classical theism believes in a single creator God who is distinct from the world, sustains it, and can actively engage with it. Deism holds that the world operates according to its own laws without divine intervention. Pantheism affirms that God is identical to the world, while panentheism maintains that the world is part of God. Other classifications include process theism, open theism, theistic finitism, and skeptical theism.
Many arguments for and against theism are discussed in the academic literature. Ontological arguments rely on pure reasoning, for example, by deducing the existence of God from the concept of God. Cosmological arguments affirm that a first cause or necessary being is required to explain the existence of the world. Teleological arguments hold that certain features of the world, such as the presence of intelligent life, indicate the existence of an intelligent designer God. Arguments from evil maintain that the presence of evil in the world undermines the claim that God exists. Science-based criticisms assert that the development of the universe and life is better explained by modern science than by religious doctrines. Other objections hold that the concept of God is incoherent or that the available evidence is insufficient to support theism.
Although theism is not itself a religion, it is a central feature of many religions, including the Abrahamic religions, Hinduism, Sikhism, and Chinese and African folk religions. It is of interest to various fields of inquiry, such as religious studies, philosophy, anthropology, and sociology. Theism has possible precursors in prehistory and is expressed in diverse religions that arose in antiquity. It evolved in various ways in subsequent history and was shaped by theological and philosophical debates about the nature and existence of God or gods.

It evolved in various ways in subsequent history and was shaped by theological and philosophical debates about the nature and existence of God or gods.


Definition
Theism is a family of views about the existence of a god or gods, but its precise definition is disputed. Understood broadly, it is the view that at least one god exists. This characterization leaves open whether there is more than one god and what divine attributes deities have. In this sense, theism contrasts with nontheism and atheism, which denote an absence or rejection of belief in a god or gods. Defined more narrowly, theism refers to the affirmation of the existence of a single god: a supreme being that is all-knowing, all-powerful, and all-benevolent. This view is sometimes associated with the beliefs that God created the world, is distinct from it, actively governs it, and is worthy of human worship. According to this narrow characterization, belief systems that characterize God differently or affirm more than one god do not belong to theism.
Some approaches characterize theism in psychological terms as a belief, while others regard it as a proposition or philosophical thesis that is either true or false, regardless of whether anyone believes it. A person who believes in theism is called a theist. Theism is a central tenet of various religions, often acting as an underlying presupposition of their worldviews and forms of life. However, it is not itself a particular religion, and a person can be a theist without belonging to an organized religion. Religious traditions typically include additional doctrines, such as teachings about moral duties, religious practices, and the afterlife, and differ in how they describe the nature, number, and roles of deities.
The term theism has its roots in the ancient Greek word θεός (theos), meaning 'god' or 'divine power'. It entered the English language in the 17th century, coined by the philosopher and theologian Ralph Cudworth in his 1678 book The True Intellectual System of the Universe.


Basic concepts


God and gods

The concept god is central to many aspects of theism, concerning both its definition and the arguments for and against it. A god is typically understood as a sacred being that possesses and exercises special powers over the natural world. Examples include Shiva in Hinduism, Ra in the ancient Egyptian religion, Zeus in the ancient Greek religion, Olodumare in the Yoruba religion, Yahweh in Judaism, the Christian God, and Allah in Islam. Gods are normally regarded as personal and conscious beings, in contrast to impersonal divine principles or forces, such as the law of karma in Buddhism. They are often seen as supernatural entities capable of influencing the natural world without being bound by its laws. The precise characterization of the nature and attributes of gods varies across traditions.
Theorists sometimes distinguish the specific concept God, spelled with an uppercase letter, from the more general concept of gods. According to this view, God is the singular highest being, either as the only existing god or as the supreme reality that includes all gods. An influential characterization, associated with perfect being theology, considers God as a supreme being with the highest degree of perfection, typically expressed in three divine attributes: omnipotence, omniscience, and omnibenevolence. Omnipotence means that God is all-powerful: they have maximal power and can do whatever is possible, without any external restraints limiting what they are capable of. Omniscience means that God is all-knowing: they have maximal knowledge and are aware of every truth without error or uncertainty, encompassing everything that was, is, and will be. Omnibenevolence means that God is maximally good: they possess ultimate kindness and generosity, and treat every being with perfect moral goodness.
Another common characterization describes God as self-existent and independent, while worldly entities are regarded as dependent on God, for example, because God created the world from nothing and actively governs it. This contrast is sometimes expressed by asserting that God exists necessarily and could not have failed to exist, while worldly entities exist contingently and could have failed to exist. Other suggested attributes include that God is eternal (without beginning and end), immutable (unchanging), omnipresent (present everywhere in the physical universe), transcendent (existing beyond the limits of the physical universe), simple (not composed of parts), incorporeal (without a body), and hidden (not directly perceivable).
Another topic concerns religious language used to describe the divine and whether it is possible, at least in principle, to give an accurate description of God or gods. Cataphatic theology argues that positive descriptions are possible: one can state what a god is like and what features they have. Apophatic theology rejects this view, proposing instead that only negative descriptions are possible: statements about what a god is not. A related discussion concerns the meaning and accuracy of religious language. The theory of univocity holds that terms used in theological descriptions, such as good and wise, have the same meaning when applied to humans and deities. Analogical theories, by contrast, hold that their meanings differ, for example, that the goodness of a deity resembles that of a human being although the two expressions do not convey the same idea.


Belief
Belief, another central term, is a mental state or subjective attitude about what is true. It contrasts with disbelief, which regards a proposition as false, and with suspension of judgment, which remains neutral and neither affirms nor rejects. Belief can vary in degree of confidence and does not require absolute certainty. Accordingly, some theists may have unquestioning confidence, whereas others may hold a tentative belief while acknowledging uncertainty. One approach analyzes belief in terms of probability: to believe a proposition is to hold that it is more likely to be true than false. Belief may be based on rational justification, such as philosophical arguments, but a person may also hold a belief without being able to justify it.
Belief is closely related to faith, but the two are not always treated as synonyms. While both belief and faith typically involve regarding something as true, faith is often understood as including additional components. For example, faith in a deity may imply trust in and personal commitment to this deity beyond the assertion that it exists. Faith is also more closely associated with practical consequences as something that guides a person's life and motivates worship and rituals, rather than remaining a purely intellectual judgment.
Belief differs from desire and hope, which are subjective attitudes about what a person wants rather than what they take to be true. Accordingly, a person who desires or hopes that God exists is not necessarily a theist if they judge God's existence unlikely.


Contrasting views
Theism contrasts with atheism, which involves an absence or rejection of belief in God or gods. Atheism is sometimes divided into negative and positive forms. Negative atheism, sometimes called non-theism, denotes a mere absence of belief. In this sense, anyone who is not a theist is an atheist, including those who have no opinion or have never considered the issue. Positive atheism, by contrast, involves an active rejection of the existence of deities, implying a disbelief rather than a suspension of judgment. Defined more abstractly, it is the philosophical thesis that there is no god.
A different classification distinguishes between global and local atheism. Global atheism is a general denial of the existence of gods, applying to all deities regardless of their exact attributes or tradition-specific characterizations. It contrasts with local atheism, which rejects a particular conception of a god, such as the conception of an all-powerful, all-knowing, and all-benevolent god. Accordingly, a person can be a theist with respect to one god conception and a local atheist with respect to another, such as a Christian believer who is a local atheist regarding Zeus.
Another common contrast is between theism and agnosticism. Agnosticism can be defined in a psychological or a philosophical sense. Understood psychologically, it is a personal suspension of judgment as a type of negative atheism. Understood philosophically, it is the thesis that the existence of God or gods is unknowable. This view goes beyond a personal suspension of judgment: it is the more general claim that no one, neither oneself nor others, can know, for example, because the evidence for and against balances out or because there is no evidence either way. In this sense, agnosticism is sometimes regarded as a rejection of both theism and positive atheism by challenging the assumption that knowledge is possible. However, there is also a sense in which agnosticism and theism can be combined: an agnostic theist is someone who believes in a god while denying that knowledge can be achieved.
When theism is defined in a narrow sense as the belief in a single supreme being that differs from and actively governs the world, it contrasts with other beliefs about gods. For example, it contrasts with polytheism, which believes in more than one god; with deism, which holds that God does not intervene in the world after creating it; and with pantheism, which holds that God is identical to the world.

grok_lead: Theism is the belief in the existence of at least one deity, typically conceived as a personal God who possesses attributes of perfection, including unlimited knowledge (omniscience), power (omnipotence), and moral goodness (omnibenevolence), and who acts as the creator and sustainer of the universe. The term "theism" derives from the Greek word theos, meaning "god," and was first introduced in the 17th century by the English philosopher Ralph Cudworth (1617â1688) to denote a worldview affirming divine existence in contrast to atheism and emerging deistic ideas. In classical theism, often associated with Anselmian traditions, God is understood as a necessary being whose essence entails these perfections, independent of the created order and eternally existent. This framework has profoundly influenced Western philosophy and theology, underpinning arguments for God 's existenceâsuch as ontological, cosmological, and teleological proofsâwhile also sparking debates on issues like the problem of evil, divine hiddenness, and the compatibility of omniscience with human free will. Theism encompasses various forms, including monotheism (belief in one God, as in Judaism, Christianity, and Islam), but excludes non-interventionist views like deism, where God creates but does not sustain or interact with the world. Historically, theistic thought traces back to ancient philosophical inquiries, evolving through medieval scholasticism âexemplified by thinkers like Thomas Aquinas âand into modern analytic philosophy, where renewed interest since the mid-20th century has arisen from critiques of logical positivism and advances in modal logic supporting the coherence of divine attributes. Key concepts in theism emphasize God's transcendence (beyond the physical world) yet immanence (active within creation), the relational nature of divine-human interaction through prayer and revelation, and the implications for ethics, where moral obligations derive from God's nature or commands. Contemporary variants, such as process theism, challenge classical immutability by portraying God as dynamically responsive to the world, reflecting ongoing philosophical refinement.
